If you sell digital products, these are 3 legal documents you need to know about, and most sellers completely overlook number 3 👀 1️⃣ Digital Product Purchase Agreement This can establish the terms of the purchase, including restrictions on sharing or reselling your digital product and other important purchase terms. 2️⃣ Website/Store Terms & Conditions Your Terms & Conditions establish the rules for your online business and can address things like refunds, intellectual property, and limitations of liability. 3️⃣ Content Usage License If a brand or client pays to use your videos, templates, graphics, courses, or other content, a content usage license can clearly define how they can use it, where, for how long, and what happens if they go beyond those rights. Your creativity is an asset. Treat it like one. 💅🏾 And no, you don't necessarily need to spend hundreds on legal fees just to get foundational documents in place. Your digital product checkout is more than a payment button. 👀 If you sell ebooks, templates, courses, guides, Canva templates, or other digital products, you need to think about what happens after someone clicks “buy.” Before selling your first digital product, make sure you have: 1️⃣ Purchase terms — what the customer is actually agreeing to when they buy. 2️⃣ License & use restrictions — what they can and cannot do with your product. 3️⃣ Privacy Policy — especially if you’re collecting customer information. 4️⃣ Website/store terms — the rules governing purchases and use of your store. 5️⃣ Protection against unauthorized sharing & reselling — because your digital product should not become the internet’s free download. 😭 Your creativity is an asset. Treat it like one. And remember: your legal protection shouldn’t start after someone steals or misuses your digital product. It should be part of your business from the beginning. When I first heard “digital product,” I think I pictured one thing: A giant e-book. Something I'd have to spend months creating before anyone could buy it. Turns out... digital products can be MUCH simpler than that. 😄 A digital product could be: → a checklist → a template → a planner → a tracker → a workbook → a spreadsheet → a swipe file → a printable → a short guide → a mini training But here's the part I'm learning matters more than the format: It needs to HELP someone. That's it. The 97-page e-book isn't automatically more valuable than the one-page checklist. If that checklist saves someone an hour... helps her make a decision... shows her what to do next... or makes something confusing easier... it has value. And this connects to something I shared a few days ago: I'm learning not to start with: “What product could I make?” Start with: “What problem could I help solve?” THEN ask what format would make that solution easiest to use. Maybe she needs a guide. Maybe she needs a template. Maybe she just needs the exact checklist you wish someone had handed YOU. I'm still learning how to create and sell digital products myself. But understanding this made the whole idea feel much less intimidating. You don't necessarily need to create something HUGE. Create something USEFUL. More Freedom. Less Fame.
